The patient is an 82-year-old male seen in the geriatrics clinic for follow-up of osteoporosis after a fragility fracture. Four months ago he slipped on a wet kitchen floor and fractured his left distal radius, which was treated in a cast. A bone density scan done after the fracture showed a T-score of -2.9 at the femoral neck. He has never been treated for osteoporosis and takes no regular medications. He does not smoke and drinks one beer a week.

Today he reports mild aching in the left wrist when he lifts heavy pots, but the fracture has otherwise healed well. He denies any new falls since the injury, hip pain, back pain, and loss of height. He also denies dizziness on standing.

On examination, blood pressure was 128/76, heart rate 72, and weight 70 kg. The left wrist showed a healed fracture with mild tenderness over the distal radius and full range of motion. The spine was non-tender, and his gait was steady without an assistive device. Labs from last week showed calcium 9.4 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D 18 ng/mL, which is low.

My impression is osteoporosis after a fragility fracture of the distal radius, with vitamin D insufficiency. I started alendronate 70 mg once weekly and vitamin D3 1,000 units daily. We reviewed how to take alendronate with a full glass of water and to stay upright for 30 minutes afterward. I advised him to see his dentist before starting long-term therapy, and I ordered a repeat bone density scan in two years. He will return in three months to review how he is tolerating the medication and to repeat his vitamin D level.

Emergency department provider dictation. The patient is a 65-year-old male who presented with right lower quadrant abdominal pain that began yesterday evening around the umbilicus and over about twelve hours moved to the right lower quadrant. He describes the pain as sharp and constant, eight out of ten, worse with walking and coughing. He has had nausea and loss of appetite since this morning. He denies vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, blood in the stool, dysuria, hematuria, and testicular pain. He also denies chest pain and shortness of breath. Past medical history is hypertension and type 2 diabetes, and he has had no prior abdominal surgery. Home medications are lisinopril 20 mg daily and metformin 1000 mg twice daily. Allergies, and this is important, he reports an allergy to ibuprofen with hives and facial swelling, and says the same happens with naproxen, so we are avoiding NSAIDs.

Vital signs at triage, blood pressure 152 over 88, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 18, temperature 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit, correction, 100.2 degrees Fahrenheit on recheck, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. On exam he is uncomfortable but nontoxic appearing. Heart and lungs are normal. The abdomen is soft with focal tenderness over McBurney's point, voluntary guarding, and rebound tenderness in the right lower quadrant, with no rigidity and no distension. Rovsing sign is positive. Testicular and hernia exams are normal.

ED course. Labs show white blood cell count 14.8 with neutrophil predominance, hemoglobin 14.2, creatinine 1.0, glucose 168, and a normal lactate. Urinalysis shows no blood and no signs of infection. CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast shows a dilated appendix measuring 12 millimeters with periappendiceal fat stranding and a small appendicolith, with no abscess, no perforation, and no free air. He received a liter of normal saline, morphine 4 mg IV, acetaminophen 1000 mg IV, ondansetron 4 mg IV, ceftriaxone 2 g IV, and metronidazole 500 mg IV. Pain improved to three out of ten after treatment.

Medical decision making. This is acute uncomplicated appendicitis. Ureteral stone is less likely given the clean urinalysis and CT, and diverticulitis is not seen on imaging. Because he received IV contrast and has diabetes, I am holding the metformin and starting sliding scale insulin while he is in the hospital. Lisinopril will continue at the home dose.

Disposition. General surgery has evaluated the patient and he will be admitted for laparoscopic appendectomy. He is NPO. Continue ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours and metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours. Continue morphine 4 mg IV as needed for pain. Avoid NSAIDs. Repeat creatinine in the morning.

note:
Visit modality: secure video visit. The patient joined from home with good audio and video, and identity and location were confirmed.

Reason for visit: Follow-up of pulmonary embolism on anticoagulation in a 76-year-old female.

Interval history: The patient was diagnosed with a pulmonary embolism three months ago and has been taking apixaban 5 mg twice daily since the initial treatment phase. Since the last visit she traveled internationally for ten days, with an 11-hour flight each way, and returned four days ago. She wore compression stockings and walked the aisle during both flights. Because of the time zone change she missed two doses of apixaban on the outbound trip. She reports mild right calf achiness since the return flight, which is slowly improving. She took naproxen 220 mg twice daily for about three days during the trip for the achiness. She also gets winded climbing one flight of stairs, which is unchanged from before the trip. She denies calf swelling, chest pain, hemoptysis, lightheadedness, and fainting. She also denies black stools, blood in the urine, nosebleeds, and bleeding gums. She takes amlodipine 5 mg daily for hypertension.

Home measurements: blood pressure 134/78, heart rate 76, oxygen saturation 96% on room air by home fingertip oximeter, and temperature 98.2 F.

Limited video examination: She appears comfortable, speaks in full sentences, and has no visible respiratory distress or audible wheeze. She showed both lower legs to the camera; there is no visible swelling, redness, or skin change, and the calves look symmetric. No bruising is seen on her forearms or hands.

Recent results: Labs from last month showed hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL.

Impression: Pulmonary embolism three months into anticoagulation, clinically stable after international travel but with two missed apixaban doses. Right calf achiness after prolonged air travel, and deep vein thrombosis needs to be excluded because anticoagulation was interrupted. Naproxen use on top of apixaban raises bleeding risk. Hypertension, stable by home readings.

Recommendations: Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily without interruption and set phone alarms for dose times. Stop naproxen. Start acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for the calf discomfort. Right leg venous duplex ultrasound within 24 hours at the hospital imaging department. Repeat complete blood count and basic metabolic panel this week at her local lab. Continue amlodipine 5 mg daily. In-person visit in four weeks to decide on the duration of anticoagulation and reassess her exertional breathlessness, with an echocardiogram if it has not improved. She should go to the emergency department for chest pain, coughing blood, fainting, or heavy bleeding.

Doctor: Hi there, come on in and have a seat. I'm the doctor at urgent care today. I see in your paperwork that you're a 59-year-old female with a kidney transplant. What brings you in?
Patient: Hi. Um, my legs have been swelling up for about a week, like really puffy. And I'm tired all the time. And the last couple of days I'm barely peeing.
Doctor: Okay, barely peeing, so much less than usual?
Patient: Yeah, way less. Maybe two times a day.
Doctor: Any burning when you go, or fever, or chills?
Patient: No burning. No fever, no chills.
Doctor: Any pain over the transplant, here on the right lower belly?
Patient: No, no pain there. I do feel sick to my stomach in the mornings, and I've had a dull headache.
Doctor: Any vomiting, chest pain, or trouble breathing?
Patient: No vomiting. No chest pain. I get a little winded on stairs, but I figured that's the swelling.
Doctor: Got it. When did you last see your transplant team?
Patient: Oh gosh, like eight months ago? I keep missing appointments. I don't have a car anymore, the bus takes two transfers and about three hours each way, and my ride cancelled on me twice.
Doctor: I hear you, that's a real barrier, and we're going to work on it today. Let's go through your medicines. What are you taking for the transplant?
Patient: Tacrolimus, 2 milligrams in the morning and 2 at night. And the mycophenolate, the 500, twice a day. And the little prednisone, the 5.
Doctor: So tacrolimus 2 mg twice a day, mycophenolate 500 mg twice a day, and prednisone 5 mg once a day?
Patient: Yes. Wait, hold on, let me look at the bottle. Hm, it says 3 milligrams. Yeah, 3 milligrams twice a day. Sorry, I mix them up.
Doctor: No problem, thanks for checking. So tacrolimus 3 mg twice a day. Have you been missing doses?
Patient: Some. I ran out about a week ago because I couldn't get to the pharmacy, so I skipped the evening ones to stretch it.
Doctor: That's important to know. Any other pills, including over the counter?
Patient: Amlodipine 5 mg for my high blood pressure. And ibuprofen for my back, the 200s, probably three or four a day for the last couple of weeks.
Doctor: Okay, so ibuprofen 200 mg, three or four a day. That is hard on any kidney, especially a transplanted one, so we'll stop that. Can I ask about alcohol?
Patient: Um, yeah, I drink. Maybe six beers a day, more on weekends. I know it's a lot.
Doctor: Thank you for being honest. When was your last drink?
Patient: Last night.
Doctor: Do your hands shake when you go without?
Patient: Sometimes in the morning, yeah.
Doctor: Alright, let me examine you. Your blood pressure is 168/96, heart rate 92, temperature 98.9, and oxygen level 97% on room air. Your legs have 2+ pitting edema up to the knees on both sides. Lungs are clear, heart is regular, and the belly over the transplant is soft and not tender. I do see a mild tremor in your hands. We ran a quick blood test: creatinine is 2.1, and your last one on record was 1.4, potassium is 5.0, and glucose is 98. Your urine dipstick shows 2+ protein, no blood, and no signs of infection.
Patient: Is that bad? Is the kidney failing?
Doctor: It's a bump in kidney function, so I'm calling it acute kidney injury on your transplant. The likely causes are the ibuprofen and the missed tacrolimus doses, and I can't rule out rejection yet, which is why we need a tacrolimus level. The amount of alcohol you're drinking is also a concern, and it looks like alcohol use disorder to me.
Patient: Oh no.
Doctor: It's treatable, and you did the right thing coming in. Here is the plan. I spoke with the on-call transplant kidney doctor, and we're drawing a tacrolimus level today before your next dose. You'll have a repeat creatinine and potassium in 2 days at the lab near your house. Stop the ibuprofen completely, and use acetaminophen 500 mg up to three times a day for your back instead. Your blood pressure is high, so increase the amlodipine to 10 mg once a day. Please keep taking tacrolimus 3 mg, mycophenolate 500 mg, and prednisone 5 mg exactly as prescribed. We'll send a 2 week supply of each to a pharmacy that delivers to your door. I'm also starting thiamine 100 mg once a day and folic acid 1 mg once a day for the alcohol, and our social worker will meet you before you leave to set up a ride service for the transplant clinic and a video visit with the transplant team in 2 days.
Patient: Okay. What about the drinking?
Doctor: Cutting down suddenly can be dangerous, so don't stop cold on your own. The social worker will connect you with an addiction counselor, and the transplant team will talk to you about it too. If you vomit, stop peeing, get short of breath, have chest pain, or the shaking gets worse, go to the emergency department right away.
Patient: Okay, I understand. 3 milligrams twice a day, no ibuprofen, 10 for the pressure.
Doctor: Perfect. That's exactly right.
summary: A 59-year-old female with a kidney transplant presented to urgent care with a week of leg swelling, fatigue, nausea, headache, and reduced urine output. She has missed transplant follow-up for eight months because of transportation barriers, ran out of tacrolimus, took ibuprofen several times daily, and drinks about six beers a day. Examination showed blood pressure 168/96, 2+ pitting edema to the knees, and a mild tremor, with creatinine 2.1 compared with a prior 1.4 and potassium 5.0. The impression was acute kidney injury on the transplant with alcohol use disorder. Ibuprofen was stopped, a tacrolimus level and repeat labs were arranged, amlodipine was increased to 10 mg daily, and social work will arrange transport and a video visit.

The patient is a 37-year-old female seen in the psychiatry clinic for follow-up of major depressive disorder and medication management. Her medical history includes hypothyroidism, type 2 diabetes, and migraine headaches. She completed the ninth grade and told me that reading medication labels is hard for her, so she identifies her pills by color and shape. Because of this, I used plain words, a picture-based pill card, and teach-back throughout the visit, asking her to repeat each instruction in her own words.

Eight weeks ago her bupropion was stopped because it made her jittery and worsened her anxiety, and sertraline was started and later raised. Today she says her mood is somewhat better than at the last visit but still low most days. She reports poor sleep, low energy, trouble concentrating, and decreased appetite. She still enjoys time with her children, which she did not at the last visit. She denies suicidal thoughts, thoughts of harming others, hearing voices, and episodes of unusually high energy. She denies panic attacks and drinking alcohol. Her migraines occur about twice a month and respond to sumatriptan.

Medication review was difficult. She first told me she takes sertraline 50 mg every morning, the small white pill. She had brought her bottles, and when we read the sertraline label together it states 100 mg once daily, and she confirmed that she takes one tablet each morning. So her current dose is sertraline 100 mg daily. She also takes trazodone 50 mg at bedtime for sleep, levothyroxine 88 mcg every morning, metformin 500 mg twice daily with meals, and sumatriptan 50 mg as needed for migraine. She admitted that she often skips the evening metformin because she forgets, which we discussed gently.

On examination, blood pressure was 122/76 and heart rate 78. Weight was 82 kg. She was neatly groomed, cooperative, and mildly dysphoric with a restricted range of affect. Speech was normal in rate and volume. Thought process was linear, with no delusions or hallucinations. She denied suicidal ideation, and insight and judgment were fair. The PHQ-9 score was 14, down from 21 eight weeks ago. Her TSH last month was 2.4 mIU/L and her hemoglobin A1c was 6.9%.

My impression is major depressive disorder, recurrent, moderate, with a partial response to sertraline 100 mg daily. Her hypothyroidism is well controlled by the TSH, her diabetes is controlled with an A1c of 6.9%, and her migraines are stable.

For the plan, I increased sertraline from 100 mg to 150 mg once daily. To avoid mix-ups, I will send a new prescription for 50 mg tablets with instructions to take three tablets each morning, and she will bring the old 100 mg bottle to the pharmacy to be discarded. Trazodone 50 mg at bedtime, levothyroxine, metformin, and sumatriptan will continue unchanged. I asked the pharmacy to put her morning and evening pills in blister packs labeled with pictures of the sun and moon, and she will use a pill box until they arrive. I referred her to the clinic therapist for cognitive behavioral therapy and gave her the crisis line information in writing with large print, and she repeated back when to use it. She will return in four weeks, sooner if her mood worsens or she has any thoughts of harming herself.

Doctor: Welcome back. Tell me what you've been feeling.
Patient: It burns when I pee, I have to go all the time, and my lower belly aches. My urine looks dark and cloudy. I felt warm one night too.
Doctor: Any blood in the urine, back pain, vomiting, or new confusion?
Patient: No blood, no back pain, no vomiting. I'm just tired.
Family member: She's been sharp as ever, no confusion.
Doctor: Good. Tell me about the trip.
Patient: Fourteen hours on the plane each way. I didn't drink much because I didn't want to use the bathroom on the plane, and where we stayed the bathroom was far from my room, so I held it a lot.
Doctor: That can set off an infection. What treatment did you get over there?
Patient: A clinic gave me ciprofloxacin. I took it for three days and stopped when I felt better.
Family member: Mom, it was five days, you finished the whole box. It was 500 milligrams twice a day for five days.
Patient: Oh, that's right, five days.
Doctor: Okay, so ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice a day for five days, and the symptoms came back about three days after you finished. Your primary doctor sent a urine culture last week, and the result is back. It grew ESBL E. coli, which is resistant to ciprofloxacin and to many of the usual oral antibiotics, but it is still sensitive to fosfomycin.
Patient: Is that bad?
Doctor: It's treatable. Let me go over your history first. You have atrial fibrillation, high blood pressure, stage 3 kidney disease, and arthritis, right?
Patient: Yes, that's right.
Doctor: And your medicines?
Patient: The apixaban for my heart rhythm, 2.5 mg twice a day. Amlodipine 5 mg every morning. Acetaminophen when my knees hurt. The oxybutynin for my bladder, 5 mg twice a day. And the estrogen cream, twice a week.
Doctor: That's estradiol vaginal cream, 0.5 g twice a week, correct?
Patient: Yes.
Doctor: Let me examine you. Temperature is 99.4, blood pressure 138/74, heart rate 78, and oxygen level 97% on room air. Your lower belly is mildly tender right above the pubic bone, and there's no tenderness over the kidneys in your back. Lungs are clear, and your heart rhythm is irregular, which is your known atrial fibrillation. We did a bladder scan, and after you urinated you still had 180 mL left in the bladder, which is more than we'd like. Your kidney labs show creatinine 1.4 and an eGFR of 36, and the kidney and bladder ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis and no stones.
Patient: What does it mean that I'm not emptying?
Doctor: The oxybutynin can make the bladder muscle lazy and trap urine, which feeds infections, especially at your age. So you have a urinary tract infection with ESBL E. coli, and your bladder isn't emptying completely. I want to stop the oxybutynin.
Patient: But then I'll leak.
Doctor: We'll watch for that, and if you need something else, we have options that don't cause retention. Here's the plan. For the infection, you'll take a 3 g dose of fosfomycin by mouth tonight and another in three days, which is safe at your kidney function. Stop the oxybutynin. Increase the estradiol cream to 0.5 g every night for two weeks, then back to twice a week, which helps keep the tissue healthy and lowers infection risk. Drink more fluids, about six glasses a day, and try to empty your bladder every three hours while awake, sitting all the way back and waiting a moment before you stand up. I'll also put a note in your chart about the resistant bacteria so future antibiotics are chosen with that in mind. I want a repeat bladder scan and a visit in 4 weeks, and if the infections continue, we'll look inside the bladder with a cystoscopy.
Family member: Should she still take the apixaban?
Doctor: Yes, keep taking apixaban 2.5 mg twice a day. Fosfomycin doesn't interact with it, and nothing changes there.
Patient: Okay, so no more oxybutynin, the cream every night for two weeks, and the antibiotic tonight.
Doctor: Exactly right. Please come back sooner or go to the emergency room if you get a high fever, shaking chills, vomiting, can't pass urine, or become confused.

Dermatology inpatient consultation dictation. Requested by the hospitalist service for evaluation of a changing pigmented lesion. The patient is a 53-year-old female on hospital day 3 for cellulitis of the right lower leg. At the skin check on admission, the nurse noticed a dark mole on her left upper back, and the patient says her husband has told her it has been getting bigger and darker over about six months. She says it has been itchy and bled once after she scratched it. She denies pain from the lesion, new moles elsewhere, and unintentional weight loss. She has fair skin, burns easily, and had several blistering sunburns as a teenager. No prior skin cancer. She works as a night-shift nurse on a rotating schedule and sleeps during the day, so she has trouble attending morning appointments and has not had a full skin exam in many years.

Past history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hypothyroidism. Current inpatient medications are cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours, lisinopril 10 mg daily, which was reduced from 20 mg by the primary team because her blood pressures were soft on admission, levothyroxine 100 mcg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and insulin sliding scale. Her home metformin 1000 mg twice daily is on hold while she is in the hospital, and vancomycin was stopped on hospital day 2 after the MRSA nasal swab was negative. No known drug allergies.

Vitals today are blood pressure 122/74, heart rate 76, and temperature 98.2 F. Labs show white blood cell count 9.8, down from 13.4 on admission, creatinine 0.9, and hemoglobin A1c 7.4%. On exam, there is a pigmented lesion on the left upper back measuring 7 mm in greatest diameter, correction, 9 mm on repeat measurement with a ruler. It is asymmetric with an irregular, notched border and variegated color with shades of brown, black, and a focal area of blue-gray. The center is slightly raised with a small crusted erosion. There is no ulceration and no active bleeding. Dermoscopy shows an atypical network, irregular streaks, and a blue-white veil. There is no lymphadenopathy in the axillae, neck, or groin. The rest of the full skin exam shows about twenty benign-appearing nevi and no other atypical lesions. The erythema of the right lower leg is receding.

My impression is a changing pigmented lesion on the left upper back, 9 mm, with asymmetry, border irregularity, color variegation, diameter over 6 mm, and evolution, suspicious for melanoma versus a severely dysplastic nevus. The cellulitis is improving.

Procedure and recommendations. I explained the concern to the patient and obtained verbal consent. I performed a bedside excisional biopsy today using an elliptical excision with 2 mm margins under 3 mL of 1% lidocaine with epinephrine, closed with nylon sutures, well tolerated, with minimal bleeding. Send to dermatopathology with a request for Breslow thickness if melanoma is confirmed. Keep the site dry for 48 hours. Sutures will be removed in 14 days in the dermatology clinic, and because of her night shifts we will schedule a late-afternoon appointment and call her with the pathology result at a time she chooses. If melanoma is confirmed, she will need wide local excision and a discussion of sentinel lymph node biopsy with surgical oncology. Full skin exams every six months afterward, with daily sunscreen and sun protection counseling. Continue antibiotics and diabetes management per the primary team.

Doctor: Hello, come in and have a seat. I see you're a 69-year-old female here for a painful toe. What happened?
Patient: Oh, doctor, my right big toe started throbbing two nights ago and woke me up at three in the morning. Now it's red, puffy, and hot, and I can't even let a sheet touch it.
Doctor: How bad is the pain, zero to ten?
Patient: A nine. I could hardly walk in here.
Doctor: Any fever or chills? Any other joints involved?
Patient: No fever, no chills. Just the toe. My right ankle is a little stiff, but nothing like the toe.
Doctor: Any injury to the foot?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Have you had this before?
Patient: Twice. The last time was about a year ago. That's when they told me it was gout and started me on allopurinol.
Doctor: How much allopurinol are you taking?
Patient: 300 milligrams once a day. Wait, let me check my pill list. No, it says 100 milligrams. I thought it was the 300. So 100 once a day, sorry.
Doctor: Thanks for checking. So allopurinol 100 mg once a day. What else do you take?
Patient: Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg for my high blood pressure, metformin 500 mg twice a day for sugar, atorvastatin 20 mg at night, and I've been taking over-the-counter naproxen, 2 tablets twice a day, for the toe for two days.
Doctor: Those are 220 mg tablets, so naproxen 220 mg, 2 tablets twice a day, correct?
Patient: Yes.
Doctor: Do you smoke?
Patient: Yes, about a pack a day for 40 years. I've tried to quit but it never sticks.
Doctor: Alcohol?
Patient: Just a glass of wine on weekends.
Doctor: Okay, let me examine you. Blood pressure is 146/88, heart rate 88, temperature 98.9. Your right big toe joint is swollen, red, warm, and very tender to even a light touch. The right ankle looks normal with full movement, and I don't see any tophi, which are chalky lumps under the skin. Your labs from this morning show uric acid 9.1, creatinine 1.3 with an eGFR of 44, and hemoglobin A1c 6.8%. The foot x-ray shows swelling of the soft tissue at the big toe joint but no erosions.
Patient: So it's gout again?
Doctor: Yes, an acute gout flare in the right big toe, and your kidneys are mildly reduced, stage 3 kidney disease. Two things are making it worse: the hydrochlorothiazide, which raises uric acid, and the allopurinol dose is too low to protect you. Smoking also makes everything worse.
Patient: What do we do?
Doctor: Here's the plan. Stop the naproxen, because with your kidneys and blood pressure it's not safe. Start prednisone 30 mg once a day for 5 days with breakfast, and since you have diabetes, check your sugars twice a day while you're on it. Stop the hydrochlorothiazide and switch to amlodipine 5 mg once a day for your high blood pressure. Increase the allopurinol from 100 mg to 200 mg once a day, and I'm adding colchicine 0.6 mg once a day for the next 3 months to prevent flares while the allopurinol builds up. We'll recheck your uric acid and kidney function in 4 weeks, and the goal is a uric acid below 6. For the smoking, I'd like you to try a nicotine patch 21 mg once a day, and I'll refer you to the quitline.
Patient: I'll try the patch. Do I keep taking the metformin and the atorvastatin?
Doctor: Yes, those continue unchanged, metformin 500 mg twice a day and atorvastatin 20 mg at night. Drink plenty of water, elevate the foot, and use ice packs for comfort. Call us if you get a fever, if the pain isn't better in 3 days, or if other joints swell up.
Patient: Okay. Prednisone for 5 days, no naproxen, amlodipine instead of the water pill, and 200 of the allopurinol.
Doctor: That's exactly right. See you back in 4 weeks.
